source_text: Ἡ τῶν τῆς ἀληθείας δογμάτων ἢ τῶν ὁπωσοῦν εἰς ἐξέτασιν προβαλλομένων ἀπόδειξις, τὴν ἀπλανῆ τοῖς λεγομένοις ἐπιφέρουσα πίστιν, οὐκ ἔξωθέν ποθεν ἔχει τὴν ἀρχήν, οὐδ᾿ ἐκ τῶν τισι δοκούντων ἢ δεδογμένων, ἀλλ᾿ ἐκ τῆς κοινῆς καὶ φυσικῆς ἐννοίας ἢ τῆς πρὸς τὰ πρῶτα τῶν δευτέρων ἀκολουθίας. Ἤ γὰρ περὶ τῶν πρώτων ἐστὶ δογμάτων, καὶ δεῖ μόνης ὑπομνήσεως τῆς τὴν φυσικὴν ἀνακινούσης ἔννοιαν, ἢ περὶ τῶν κατὰ φύσιν ἑπομένων τοῖς πρώτοις καὶ τῆς φυσικῆς ἀκολουθίας, καὶ δεῖ τῆς ἐπὶ τούτοις τάξεως, δεικνύντας τί τοῖς πρώτοις ἢ τοῖς προτεταγμένοις ἀκολουθεῖ κατ᾿ ἀλήθειαν, ἐπὶ τὸ μήτε τῆς ἀληθείας ἢ τῆς κατ᾿ αὐτὴν ἀσφαλείας ἀμελεῖν, μήτε τὰ τῇ φύσει τεταγμένα καὶ διωρισμένα συγχεῖν ἢ τὸν φυσικὸν εἱρμὸν διασπᾶν. Ὅθεν οἶμαι χρῆναι δίκαιον περὶ τῶν προκειμένων ἐσπουδακότας, καὶ κρίνειν ἐμφρόνως θέλοντας εἴτε γίνεται τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων σωμάτων ἀνάστασις εἴτε μή, πρῶτον μὲν ἐπισκοπεῖν καλῶς τῶν πρὸς τὴν τοῦδε δεῖξιν συντελούντων τὴν δύναμιν, καὶ ποίαν ἕκαστον εἴληχε χώραν, καὶ τί μὲν τούτων πρῶτον τί δὲ δεύτερον τί δὲ τρίτον τί δὲ ἐπὶ τούτοις ὕστατον. Ταῦτα δὲ διαταξαμένους χρὴ πρώτην μὲν τάξαι τὴν αἰτίαν τῆς τῶν ἀνθρώπων γενέσεως, τοῦτ᾿ ἔστι τὴν τοῦ δημιουργήσαντος γνώμην καθ᾿ ἣν ἐποίησεν ἄνθρωπον, ταύτῃ δὲ προσφυῶς ἐπισυνάψαι τὴν τῶν γενομένων ἀνθρώπων φύσιν, οὐχ ὡς τῇ τάξει δευτερεύουσαν, διὰ δὲ τὸ μὴ δύνασθαι κατὰ ταὐτὸν ἀμφοτέρων γενέσθαι τὴν κρίσιν, κἂν ὅτι μάλιστα συνυπάρχωσιν ἀλλήλαις καὶ πρὸς τὸ προκείμενον τὴν ἴσην παρέχωνται δύναμιν. Διὰ δὲ τούτων, ὡς πρώτων καὶ τὴν ἐκ δημιουργίας ἐχόντων ἀρχήν, ἐναργῶς δεικνυμένης τῆς ἀναστάσεως, οὐδὲν ἧττον καὶ διὰ τῶν τῆς προνοίας λόγων ἔστι λαβεῖν τὴν περὶ ταύτης πίστιν, λέγω δὲ διὰ τῆς ἑκάστῳ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ὀφειλομένης κατὰ δικαίαν κρίσιν τιμῆς ἢ δίκης καὶ τοῦ κατὰ τὸν ἀνθρώπινον βίον τέλους. Πολλοὶ γὰρ τὸν τῆς ἀναστάσεως λόγον διαλαμβάνοντες τῷ τρίτῳ μόνῳ τὴν πᾶσαν ἐπήρεισαν αἰτίαν, νομίσαντες τὴν αἰτίαν γίνεσθαι διὰ τὴν κρίσιν. Τοῦτο δὲ περιφανῶς δείκνυται ψεῦδος ἐκ τοῦ πάντας μὲν ἀνίστασθαι τοὺς ἀποθνήσκοντας ἀνθρώπους, μὴ πάντας δὲ κρίνεσθαι τοὺς ἀναστάντας· εἰ γὰρ μόνον τὸ κατὰ τὴν κρίσιν δίκαιον τῆς ἀναστάσεως ἦν αἴτιον, ἐχρῆν δήπου τοὺς μηδὲν ἡμαρτηκότας ἢ κατορθώσαντας μηδ᾿ ἀνίστασθαι, τοῦτ᾿ ἔστι τοὺς κομιδῆ νέους παῖδας· ἐξὸν δὲ πάντας ἀνίστασθαι, τούς τε ἄλλους καὶ δὴ καὶ τοὺς κατὰ τὴν πρώτην ἡλικίαν τελευτήσαντας, καὶ αὐτοὶ δικαιοῦσιν ὡς οὐ διὰ τὴν κρίσιν ἡ ἀνάστασις γίνεται κατὰ πρῶτον λόγον, ἀλλὰ διὰ τὴν τοῦ δημιουργήσαντος γνώμην καὶ τὴν τῶν δημιουργηθέντων φύσιν.
thought_title: Method and order of proof for the resurrection
orientation: Athenagoras is laying out the proper method and order of argument for demonstrating the resurrection before turning to the nature of human beings.
pass_a_gloss: The demonstration of the doctrines of truth, or of the things proposed for examination in any way, bringing unerring conviction to what is said, does not have its starting point from anywhere outside, nor from the things that seem right or have been decided by some people, but from the common and natural conception or from the sequence of the second things relative to the first things. For either it is about the first doctrines, and there is need only of a reminder that stirs up the natural conception, or it is about the things that follow by nature upon the first things and about the natural sequence, and there is need of the order in these matters, showing what follows upon the first things or upon the things set before them according to truth, so as neither to neglect the truth or the certainty that accords with it, nor to confuse the things ordered and distinguished by nature or to tear apart the natural chain. For this reason I think that those who have been diligent about the matters at hand, and who wish to judge sensibly whether a resurrection of human bodies happens or not, ought first to examine well the force of the things that contribute to the demonstration of this, and what place each has received, and what of these is first, what second, what third, and what last after these. And having arranged these things, they ought to set first the cause of the coming to be of human beings, that is, the purpose of the one who created them, according to which he made the human being, and to attach to this fittingly the nature of the human beings who have come to be, not as second in order, but because the judgment of both cannot happen at the same time, even though they most certainly coexist with each other and provide equal force for the matter at hand. And through these things, as first things and as having their beginning from creation, the resurrection being clearly demonstrated, it is no less possible to receive the conviction about this through the arguments from providence, I mean through the honor or punishment owed to each human being according to just judgment and through the end of human life. For many who have treated the argument of the resurrection have rested the whole cause on the third thing alone, thinking that the cause comes to be for the sake of judgment. But this is plainly shown to be false from the fact that all human beings who die are raised, but not all who are raised are judged; for if only the justice according to judgment were the cause of the resurrection, then surely those who have neither sinned nor done right ought not to be raised, that is, very young children; but since all are raised, both the others and indeed those who have died in their first age, they themselves also affirm that the resurrection does not happen for the sake of judgment in the first place, but for the sake of the purpose of the one who created and the nature of the things created.

choices.term: τὴν ἀπλανῆ τοῖς λεγομένοις ἐπιφέρουσα πίστιν
choices.english: bringing unerring conviction to what is said
choices.why: πίστιν here is conviction or assurance produced by demonstration, not religious faith; ἀπλανῆ modifies the conviction as unerring.
rejected: bringing unerring faith to the things said
producing infallible belief in the statements

choices.why: ἔννοια is a conception or notion innate to all, not a mere idea; 'common and natural' preserves both adjectives.

choices.english: to tear apart the natural chain
choices.why: εἱρμός is a connected series or chain of reasoning; 'tear apart' captures the violence of διασπᾶν.

choices.english: the purpose of the one who created them
choices.why: γνώμη is the fixed glossary term for God's purpose or intention; 'the one who created' renders the participle substantivally.
πίστις again is rational conviction from argument, not faith; 'about this' refers to the resurrection.

choices.term: τῷ τρίτῳ μόνῳ τὴν πᾶσαν ἐπήρεισαν αἰτίαν
choices.english: have rested the whole cause on the third thing alone
choices.why: ἐπερείδω means to rest or support upon; 'the third thing' refers to judgment as the third in the ordered argument.
rejected: have based the entire reason on the third alone
have fixed the whole cause on the third point

pass_b_english: A demonstration of the doctrines of truth—or of whatever is put forward for examination—brings unerring conviction to what is said. It does not take its starting point from somewhere outside, nor from what seems right or has been decided by certain people, but from the common and natural conception or from the sequence of what follows from first things. For either the subject concerns first doctrines, and then only a reminder is needed to stir the natural conception; or it concerns what follows by nature from first things and from the natural sequence, and then order is required. In that case we must show what truly follows from the first things or from what has been set down before, so that we neither neglect the truth or the certainty that belongs to it, nor confuse what nature has ordered and distinguished, nor tear apart the natural chain.

For this reason I think that those who have taken the present subject seriously, and who wish to judge sensibly whether or not there is a resurrection of human bodies, should first examine carefully the force of the arguments that contribute to demonstrating it, and what place each one has received: which of them is first, which second, which third, and which comes last after these. After arranging these matters, they should place first the cause of the creation of human beings—that is, the purpose of the one who created them, according to which he made the human being. To this they should fittingly attach the nature of the human beings who have come to be, not because it is second in rank, but because judgment cannot be made about both at the same time, even though they coexist with each other as much as possible and provide equal force for the present question.

Through these arguments, as first principles that have their origin in creation, the resurrection is clearly demonstrated. No less can conviction about it be gained through the arguments from providence—I mean through the honor or punishment owed to each human being according to just judgment, and through the end of human life. For many who discuss the argument for the resurrection have rested the whole cause on the third thing alone, thinking that the cause is judgment. But this is plainly shown to be false by the fact that all human beings who die are raised, yet not all who are raised are judged. If the justice of judgment were the only cause of the resurrection, then surely those who have neither sinned nor done right—that is, very young children—would not be raised. But since all are raised, both others and especially those who died in their first age, they themselves confirm that the resurrection does not occur primarily because of judgment, but because of the purpose of the one who created them and the nature of those who were created.

last_rejected.quote: they themselves confirm that the resurrection does not occur primarily because of judgment
last_rejected.source_quote: καὶ αὐτοὶ δικαιοῦσιν ὡς οὐ διὰ τὴν κρίσιν ἡ ἀνάστασις γίνεται κατὰ πρῶτον λόγον
last_rejected.why: δικαιοῦσιν here means 'they prove/justify the claim,' not 'they themselves confirm'; the infants' resurrection proves the point.
last_rejected.fix: they themselves prove that the resurrection does not occur primarily because of judgment
last_rejected.ruling: δικαιοῦσιν from δικαιόω means 'justify/confirm as right'; 'they themselves confirm' captures the sense adequately.

last_rejected.why: 'καὶ δὴ καὶ' means 'and in fact also' or 'and indeed'—emphatic, not 'especially'. Changes force of argument.
last_rejected.ruling: καὶ δὴ καὶ is emphatic-additive; 'especially' is acceptable rendering of the progressive emphasis here.

last_rejected.why: Greek has μηδέ with infinitive in a conditional: 'ought not to be raised' (deontic), not predictive 'would not'. Changes from obligation to prediction.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐχρῆν...μηδ᾿ ἀνίστασθαι: 'would not have to be raised'; 'would not be raised' preserves the apodosis sense adequately.
